comparison: Perfect alignment on methodological claims (C35-C44). Both evaluations affirm the study's methodological approach, data sources, and comprehensive dataset. OpenEval provides technical detail about documentation while peer reviewers praise the careful use of existing data across 30 countries.

Perfect alignment on EIGE dataset findings (C97-C102). Both evaluations support the European data showing discipline effects on funding success. OpenEval provides statistical details (p<0.05, 50% relative increase) while peer reviewers accept these findings as part of the comprehensive multi-country evidence.

Perfect alignment on CIHR findings (C90, C92-C94). Both evaluations support the Canadian funding data showing discipline gender balance effects. OpenEval notes limited granularity (16 data points) while peer reviewers accept these findings within the broader multi-country context without raising concerns.

Strong alignment on PBRF detailed findings (C48-C60). Both evaluations support the temporal patterns and cross-disciplinary effects in New Zealand data. OpenEval provides extensive statistical detail across three assessment rounds while peer reviewers accept these findings as part of the convincing evidence base.

Strong alignment on ARC temporal shift findings (C81, C85-C89). Both evaluations support the Australian data showing reversal where discipline gender balance became dominant predictor by 2019. OpenEval details the statistical significance (p<0.001) while peer reviewers appreciate the temporal analysis of funding datasets.

Strong alignment on main conclusions (C110-C114) and study limitations (C103). Both evaluations support that discipline gender balance affects research evaluation for both genders. OpenEval emphasizes the correlational nature and logical inference about women being more affected; peer reviewers affirm the systemic nature extending to entire disciplines.

Partial alignment on core findings (C1, C9-C10, C30, C33). Both evaluations strongly support that female-dominated disciplines receive lower evaluations. OpenEval focuses on PBRF statistical robustness with 18,000+ data points; peer reviewers emphasize the surprising finding that men in female-dominated fields also experience lower success.

Partial alignment on bibliometric controls (C66-C67, C72, C77). Both evaluations support that discipline effects persist after controlling for publication output. OpenEval provides detailed UC subset analysis (r²=0.325) but notes limited generalizability; peer reviewers accept these controls strengthen validity without questioning the subset limitations.

Partial alignment on control variables (C4, C11, C76, C78). Both evaluations affirm that findings hold after accounting for age, outputs, and bibliometric measures. OpenEval details the UC subset analysis showing discipline balance remains significant; peer reviewers praise the comprehensive controls without examining subset-specific findings.

Partial alignment on temporal and cross-dataset patterns (C2, C31-C32). OpenEval focuses on ARC temporal shift findings; peer reviewers address broader main findings including temporal aspects. Both support that discipline gender balance is a key predictor, though evaluating different claim subsets.

Partial alignment on main conclusions (C3, C34). OpenEval evaluates the overarching conclusion about discipline effects across all datasets; peer reviewers focus on the core finding that female-dominated fields are undervalued. Both strongly support the main thesis from different analytical perspectives.

Partial alignment on control variables and conclusions (C3). Both evaluations address that discipline effects persist after controls. OpenEval emphasizes the cross-dataset consistency and correlational nature; peer reviewers specifically praise accounting for various factors including outputs and bibliometrics.

Alignment on inference about aggregate effects (C80). Both evaluations support the logical inference that more women will be adversely affected given their concentration in female-dominated fields. OpenEval notes this is an inference rather than directly tested hypothesis; peer reviewers accept this as part of the broader systemic findings.

Alignment on study limitations (C103). Both evaluations acknowledge the correlational nature of findings. OpenEval notes authors appropriately avoid causal claims; peer reviewers implicitly accept this limitation by not challenging the correlational approach and noting the study paves way for future causal research.

OpenEval evaluates background literature claims (C5-C29) establishing context about gender bias in academia. These well-cited contextual claims are not explicitly evaluated by peer reviewers, who focus on the study's original empirical contributions rather than the literature review foundation.

OpenEval evaluates mechanistic explanations (C104-C109) as appropriately speculative and cited from prior literature rather than tested in current study. Peer reviewers do not explicitly address these potential mechanisms, focusing instead on the empirical patterns demonstrated.
